claim: Out of millions of ejaculated sperm, a few reach the fertilization site in mammals.
source: Out of millions of ejaculated sperm, a few reach the fertilization site in mammals.
evidence: This is a general statement about mammalian reproduction that draws from established scientific knowledge.

claim: Flagellar Ca2+ signaling nanodomains are organized by multi-subunit CatSper calcium channel complexes.
source: Flagellar Ca2+ signaling nanodomains, organized by multi-subunit CatSper calcium channel complexes, are pivotal for sperm migration in the female tract, implicating CatSper-dependent mechanisms in sperm selection.
evidence: This statement is supported by references to prior research and is part of the established understanding of CatSper function.

claim: Flagellar Ca2+ signaling nanodomains are pivotal for sperm migration in the female tract.
source: Flagellar Ca2+ signaling nanodomains, organized by multi-subunit CatSper calcium channel complexes, are pivotal for sperm migration in the female tract, implicating CatSper-dependent mechanisms in sperm selection.
evidence: This claim is supported by the context of the study and references to prior work on CatSper function.

claim: CatSper1 is an O-linked glycosylated protein.
source: Here using biochemical and pharmacological studies, we demonstrate that CatSper1 is an O-linked glycosylated protein, undergoing capacitation-induced processing dependent on Ca2+ and phosphorylation cascades.
evidence: This claim is supported by biochemical experiments described in the manuscript, specifically enzymatic deglycosylation assays shown in Figure 1.

claim: CatSper1 undergoes capacitation-induced processing dependent on Ca2+ and phosphorylation cascades.
source: Here using biochemical and pharmacological studies, we demonstrate that CatSper1 is an O-linked glycosylated protein, undergoing capacitation-induced processing dependent on Ca2+ and phosphorylation cascades.
evidence: This claim is supported by pharmacological experiments using Ca2+ ionophores and kinase inhibitors described in the manuscript and shown in Figure 1.

claim: CatSper1 processing correlates with protein tyrosine phosphorylation (pY) development in sperm cells capacitated in vitro.
source: CatSper1 processing correlates with protein tyrosine phosphorylation (pY) development in sperm cells capacitated in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2 comparing CatSper1 and pY patterns in individual sperm cells.

claim: CatSper1 processing correlates with protein tyrosine phosphorylation (pY) development in sperm cells capacitated in vivo.
source: CatSper1 processing correlates with protein tyrosine phosphorylation (pY) development in sperm cells capacitated in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data from microdissected female tracts shown in Figure 2.

claim: Spermatozoa past the utero-tubal junction possess intact CatSper1 signals.
source: Using 3D in situ molecular imaging and ANN-based automatic detection of sperm distributed along the cleared female tract, we demonstrate that spermatozoa past the utero-tubal junction possess the intact CatSper1 signals.
evidence: This claim is supported by 3D imaging data from cleared female tracts shown in Figures 3, 4, and 6.

claim: Fertilizing mouse spermatozoa in situ are characterized by intact CatSper channel, lack of pY, and reacted acrosomes.
source: Together, we reveal that fertilizing mouse spermatozoa in situ are characterized by intact CatSper channel, lack of pY, and reacted acrosomes.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple imaging experiments shown in Figures 2, 3, and 4 examining sperm in the ampulla.

claim: Less than 100 spermatozoa are found at the fertilization site in mammals.
source: Yet less than 100 spermatozoa are found at the fertilization site, called the ampulla, and only 10–12 spermatozoa are observed around an oocyte (Kölle, 2015; Suarez, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies by Kölle (2015) and Suarez (2002).

claim: Only 10–12 spermatozoa are observed around an oocyte.
source: Yet less than 100 spermatozoa are found at the fertilization site, called the ampulla, and only 10–12 spermatozoa are observed around an oocyte (Kölle, 2015; Suarez, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies by Kölle (2015) and Suarez (2002).

claim: Surface molecules on the sperm plasma membranes such as ADAM family proteins are essential for the sperm to pass through the utero-tubal junction.
source: Recent ex vivo imaging studies combined with mouse genetics have shown that surface molecules on the sperm plasma membranes such as ADAM family proteins are essential for the sperm to pass through the utero-tubal junction (UTJ) (Fujihara et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Fujihara et al., 2018.

claim: Mammalian sperm undergo capacitation inside the oviduct.
source: Mammalian sperm undergo capacitation, a physiological process to obtain the ability to fertilize the egg, naturally inside the oviduct (Austin, 1951; Chang, 1951).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to classic studies by Austin (1951) and Chang (1951).

claim: Protein tyrosine phosphorylation (pY) showed different patterns in boar sperm capacitated in vitro from ex vivo and in vivo.
source: Protein tyrosine phosphorylation (pY), which has been utilized as a hallmark of sperm capacitation over decades, showed different patterns in boar sperm capacitated in vitro from ex vivo and in vivo (Luño et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Luño et al., 2013.

claim: In mice, pY is not required for sperm hyperactivation or fertility.
source: In mice, pY is not required for sperm hyperactivation or fertility (Alvau et al., 2016; Tateno et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Alvau et al., 2016 and Tateno et al., 2013.

claim: The sperm-specific CatSper Ca2+ channel forms multi-linear nanodomains on the flagellar membrane.
source: The sperm-specific CatSper Ca2+ channel forms multi-linear nanodomains on the flagellar membrane, functioning as a signaling hub that links these events and motility regulation during capacitation (Chung et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Chung et al., 2014.

claim: Sperm from mice lacking the CatSper genes are unable to control pY development.
source: Sperm from mice lacking the CatSper genes are unable to control pY development and fail to migrate past the UTJ (Chung et al., 2014; Ho et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chung et al., 2014 and Ho et al., 2009.

claim: Sperm from mice lacking the CatSper genes fail to migrate past the UTJ.
source: Sperm from mice lacking the CatSper genes are unable to control pY development and fail to migrate past the UTJ (Chung et al., 2014; Ho et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chung et al., 2014 and Ho et al., 2009.

claim: The presence and integrity of CatSper nanodomains correlate with sperm ability to develop hyperactivated motility.
source: The presence and integrity of CatSper nanodomains, probed by CatSper1, correlate with sperm ability to develop hyperactivated motility (Chung et al., 2017; Chung et al., 2014; Hwang et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chung et al., 2017, Chung et al., 2014, and Hwang et al., 2019.

claim: The molecular weight of CatSper1 increases gradually during sperm development and epididymal maturation.
source: Interestingly, the molecular weight of CatSper1 increases gradually during sperm development and epidydimal maturation (Figure 1A; top), indicating that CatSper1 undergoes post-translational modifications.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1A comparing CatSper1 from testis, caput, corpus, and cauda epididymis.

claim: O-glycosidase shifts the apparent molecular weight of CatSper1 to closest to the CatSper1 band that corresponds to the smallest molecular weight observed in the testis.
source: By contrast, when the sperm membrane was subjected to enzymatic deglycosylation, O-glycosidase, but not PNGase F, shifts the apparent molecular weight of CatSper1 to closest to the CatSper1 band that corresponds to the smallest molecular weight observed in the testis (Figure 1A,B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by enzymatic deglycosylation experiments shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: PNGase F does not shift the apparent molecular weight of CatSper1.
source: By contrast, when the sperm membrane was subjected to enzymatic deglycosylation, O-glycosidase, but not PNGase F, shifts the apparent molecular weight of CatSper1 to closest to the CatSper1 band that corresponds to the smallest molecular weight observed in the testis (Figure 1A,B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by enzymatic deglycosylation experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: CatSper1 in sperm is not a phosphoprotein.
source: These data suggest that CatSper1 in sperm is not a phosphoprotein but an O-linked glycosylated protein.
evidence: This claim is supported by phosphatase treatment experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: CatSper resides in lipid rafts subdomains of the plasma membrane in mature sperm.
source: CatSper resides in lipid rafts subdomains of the plasma membrane in mature sperm.
evidence: This claim is supported by sucrose density gradient centrifugation data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The molecular weight and amount of intact CatSper1 specifically declines during sperm capacitation.
source: The molecular weight and amount of intact CatSper1, among all CatSper subunits, specifically declines during sperm capacitation (Chung et al., 2014; Figure 1B,D,H,I,K).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1B, D, H, I, K and citation to Chung et al., 2014.

claim: Blocking tyrosine phosphatases by sodium orthovanadate does not change the molecular weight of CatSper1.
source: Blocking tyrosine phosphatases by sodium orthovanadate or adding specific protein phosphatases, such as protein serine/threonine phosphatase 1(PP1) or protein tyrosine phosphatase 1B (PTP1B) to solubilized sperm membrane fraction, does not change the molecular weight of CatSper1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by phosphatase treatment experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Adding protein serine/threonine phosphatase 1 (PP1) to solubilized sperm membrane fraction does not change the molecular weight of CatSper1.
source: Blocking tyrosine phosphatases by sodium orthovanadate or adding specific protein phosphatases, such as protein serine/threonine phosphatase 1(PP1) or protein tyrosine phosphatase 1B (PTP1B) to solubilized sperm membrane fraction, does not change the molecular weight of CatSper1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by phosphatase treatment experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Adding protein tyrosine phosphatase 1B (PTP1B) to solubilized sperm membrane fraction does not change the molecular weight of CatSper1.
source: Blocking tyrosine phosphatases by sodium orthovanadate or adding specific protein phosphatases, such as protein serine/threonine phosphatase 1(PP1) or protein tyrosine phosphatase 1B (PTP1B) to solubilized sperm membrane fraction, does not change the molecular weight of CatSper1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by phosphatase treatment experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Solubilized sperm lysates degrade FL-CatSper1 and result in increased detection of cleaved CatSper1.
source: Solubilized sperm lysates degrade FL-CatSper1 and result in increased detection of cleaved CatSper1 by HA antibody (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro proteolysis experiments shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Protein levels of recombinant ND-CatSper1 are not affected by incubation with sperm lysate.
source: By contrast, protein levels of recombinant ND-CatSper1 are not affected by incubation with sperm lysate (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro proteolysis experiments shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The cytoplasmic N-terminal domain of CatSper1 is the target region for proteolytic activity in sperm cells.
source: These results demonstrate that the cytoplasmic N-terminal domain of CatSper1 is the target region for proteolytic activity in sperm cells.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the differential degradation of FL-CatSper1 versus ND-CatSper1 shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Adding a PKA inhibitor H89 accelerated CatSper1 degradation during sperm capacitation.
source: Adding a PKA inhibitor H89 or the St-Ht31 peptide, which abolishes PKA anchoring to AKAP, accelerated CatSper1 degradation during sperm capacitation (Figure 1H, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The St-Ht31 peptide accelerated CatSper1 degradation during sperm capacitation.
source: Adding a PKA inhibitor H89 or the St-Ht31 peptide, which abolishes PKA anchoring to AKAP, accelerated CatSper1 degradation during sperm capacitation (Figure 1H, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Calyculin A suppresses the capacitation-associated CatSper1 degradation.
source: Consistently, calyculin A, a serine/threonine protein phosphatase inhibitor, suppresses the capacitation-associated CatSper1 degradation (Figure 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Adding Ca2+ ionophore A23187 to the sperm suspension induces CatSper1 processing even under non-capacitating conditions.
source: Interestingly, adding Ca2+ ionophore A23187 to the sperm suspension induces CatSper1 processing even under non-capacitating conditions that either do not support PKA activation or outright inhibit PKA activity (Figure 1I,J, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, top).
evidence: This claim is supported by Ca2+ ionophore experiments shown in Figure 1I, J and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: All three classes of calpain inhibitors prevent CatSper1 from capacitation-associated degradation.
source: We observed that all three classes of calpain inhibitors prevent CatSper1 from capacitation-associated degradation (Figure 1K).
evidence: This claim is supported by pharmacological experiments with calpain inhibitors shown in Figure 1K.

claim: The extent to which CatSper1 degrades varies with individual sperm cells capacitated in vitro.
source: Accordingly, the extent to which CatSper1 degrades varies with individual sperm cells capacitated in vitro (Figure 1J, Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence images showing heterogeneous CatSper1 patterns in Figure 1J and Figure 2A-C.

claim: Sperm cells that maintain intact CatSper1 develop capacitation-associated pY to a lesser degree in vitro.
source: Notably, we find that sperm cells that maintain intact CatSper1 develop capacitation-associated pY to a lesser degree in vitro (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data comparing CatSper1 and pY patterns shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: Catsper1 knockout sperm exhibit potentiated pY during capacitation.
source: This finding is consistent with the reported phenotype of Catsper1 knockout sperm that exhibit potentiated pY during capacitation (Chung et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Chung et al., 2014.

claim: CatSper1 in the spermatozoa that passed the utero-tubal junction (UTJ) are arranged normally along the tail, mostly protected from degradation.
source: By subsequent immunostaining, we found that CatSper1 in the spermatozoa that passed the utero-tubal junction (UTJ) are arranged normally along the tail, mostly protected from degradation, but in decreasing intensity and continuity more towards UTJ (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data from microdissected female tracts shown in Figure 2D.

claim: pY is not readily detected in the spermatozoa from the ampulla.
source: In striking contrast, pY is not readily detected in the spermatozoa from the ampulla but appears in the oviductal sperm increasingly towards UTJ (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data from microdissected female tracts shown in Figure 2E and F.

claim: pY appears in the oviductal sperm increasingly towards UTJ.
source: In striking contrast, pY is not readily detected in the spermatozoa from the ampulla but appears in the oviductal sperm increasingly towards UTJ (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data from microdissected female tracts shown in Figure 2E and F.

claim: Spermatozoa from the ampulla are fully capacitated and acrosome reacted.
source: Absence of EGFP reveals that spermatozoa from the ampulla are fully capacitated and acrosome reacted (AR) but those in the isthmus are undergoing AR (Figure 2D,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence imaging of Acr-EGFP sperm shown in Figure 2D and G.

claim: Spermatozoa in the isthmus are undergoing acrosome reaction.
source: Absence of EGFP reveals that spermatozoa from the ampulla are fully capacitated and acrosome reacted (AR) but those in the isthmus are undergoing AR (Figure 2D,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence imaging of Acr-EGFP sperm shown in Figure 2D and G.

claim: Acrosome reaction initiates in the mid-isthmus.
source: This result is consistent with the previous observations that AR initiates in the mid-isthmus (Hino et al., 2016; Muro et al., 2016) and reacted spermatozoa are able to penetrate the zona in vivo (Jin et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hino et al., 2016 and Muro et al., 2016.

claim: Reacted spermatozoa are able to penetrate the zona in vivo.
source: This result is consistent with the previous observations that AR initiates in the mid-isthmus (Hino et al., 2016; Muro et al., 2016) and reacted spermatozoa are able to penetrate the zona in vivo (Jin et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Jin et al., 2011.

claim: A few Catsper1-/- sperm cells that managed to arrive at the ampulla are all not acrosome reacted.
source: Interestingly, we found that a few Catsper1-/- sperm cells that managed to arrive at the ampulla are all not acrosome reacted (Figure 2H), supporting the notion that CatSper-mediated Ca2+ signaling is required for sperm acrosome reaction (Stival et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence imaging of Catsper1-/- sperm shown in Figure 2H.

claim: CatSper-mediated Ca2+ signaling is required for sperm acrosome reaction.
source: Interestingly, we found that a few Catsper1-/- sperm cells that managed to arrive at the ampulla are all not acrosome reacted (Figure 2H), supporting the notion that CatSper-mediated Ca2+ signaling is required for sperm acrosome reaction (Stival et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from Catsper1-/- sperm shown in Figure 2H and citation to Stival et al., 2018.

claim: Various tissue clearing methods are applicable to the reproductive organs from both male and female mice to preserve gross morphology, and fine cellular and subcellular structures.
source: We found that various tissue clearing methods (Chung et al., 2013; Murray et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2014) are applicable to the reproductive organs from both male and female mice to preserve gross morphology, and fine cellular and subcellular structures.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1, and citations to clearing methods.

claim: The cleared tissues preserved protein-based fluorescence.
source: The cleared tissues preserved protein-based fluorescence and were compatible with labeling with dyes and antibodies; growing follicles (WGA) inside the ovary (phalloidin), oviductal folds (WGA) and multi-ciliated (anti-Ac-Tub) epithelium (PNA), different stages of male germs cells (Acr-EGFP) in the seminiferous tubules of the testis and the epididymis are readily detected (Figure 3A–C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—videos 1–6).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence imaging of cleared tissues shown in Figure 3A-C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Two linear CatSper1 domains are easily observed in the sperm cells inside an ampullar region of the whole cleared female tract.
source: Two linear CatSper1 domains typically observed by confocal imaging are easily observed in the sperm cells inside an ampullar region of the whole cleared female tract (Figure 3I).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal imaging of cleared female tracts shown in Figure 3I.

claim: Most sperm cells located in the ampulla exhibit linearly arranged intact CatSper1 and reacted acrosomes.
source: As expected, most sperm cells located in the ampulla exhibit linearly arranged intact CatSper1 and reacted acrosomes (Figure 4A, top, Figure 4—video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal imaging of cleared female tracts shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—video 1.

claim: In the middle isthmus, both CatSper1 and acrosome remain intact in most sperm cells.
source: In the middle isthmus, both CatSper1 and acrosome remain intact in most sperm cells, but mixed patterns are observed in some cells (Figure 4A, middle, Figure 4—video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal imaging of cleared female tracts shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—video 1.

claim: Acrosome is largely intact in the sperm clusters in the proximal isthmus close to UTJ whereas CatSper1 is barely detected.
source: Interestingly, acrosome is largely intact in the sperm clusters in the proximal isthmus close to UTJ whereas CatSper1 is barely detected (Figure 4A, bottom, Figure 4—video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal imaging of cleared female tracts shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—video 1.

claim: 3D volume imaging of the mid isthmus regions reveals sperm cells aligned in one direction towards the ampulla.
source: Notably, 3D volume imaging of this mid isthmus regions reveals sperm cells aligned in one direction towards the ampulla, providing unprecedented insight into sperm taxis in the fertilization process (Figure 4—video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by 3D volume imaging shown in Figure 4—video 1.

claim: CatSper1 is largely protected from degradation once in the oviduct.
source: Our qualitative but semi-quantitative analyses suggest that CatSper1 is largely protected from degradation once in the oviduct; acrosome reaction initiates in the mid-isthmus and is completed in the ampulla before interacting with the oocytes (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of CatSper1 and acrosome patterns shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Acrosome reaction is completed in the ampulla before interacting with the oocytes.
source: Our qualitative but semi-quantitative analyses suggest that CatSper1 is largely protected from degradation once in the oviduct; acrosome reaction initiates in the mid-isthmus and is completed in the ampulla before interacting with the oocytes (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of acrosome patterns shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The selected ANN is able to recognize all the sperm detected manually.
source: The selected ANN is able to recognize all the sperm detected manually and the ANN sensitivity varies around 90% in individual samples (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C), validating the ANN performance.
evidence: This claim is supported by ANN performance evaluation shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The ANN sensitivity varies around 90% in individual samples.
source: The selected ANN is able to recognize all the sperm detected manually and the ANN sensitivity varies around 90% in individual samples (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C), validating the ANN performance.
evidence: This claim is supported by ANN performance evaluation shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C.

claim: 90% of the ANN detected sperm expresses well recognizable CatSper1 fluorescent staining patterns.
source: Furthermore, the false-negative detection of sperm all comes from the sperm with dubious signals in the antecedent human eye evaluation; the 90% of the ANN detected sperm expresses well recognizable CatSper1 fluorescent staining patterns (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by ANN detection results shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Sperm populations located along the cleared oviduct have statistically different CatSper1 quadrilateral intensity delta values.
source: Together with the whole tissue image processing (Figure 3E), the quantitative analysis clearly visualizes that sperm populations located along the cleared oviduct have statistically different CatSper1 quadrilateral intensity delta values (Figure 6H).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of CatSper1 quadrilateral organization shown in Figure 6H.

claim: Heterologously expressed CatSper1 cannot reach the plasma membrane, remaining instead at the ER/Golgi.
source: Heterologously expressed CatSper1 cannot reach the plasma membrane, remaining instead at the ER/Golgi (Chung et al., 2017; Chung et al., 2011; Ren et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chung et al., 2017, Chung et al., 2011, and Ren et al., 2001.

claim: O-linked glycosylation takes place in the cis-Golgi for secreted and transmembrane proteins after the protein is folded.
source: O-linked glycosylation takes place in the cis-Golgi for secreted and transmembrane proteins after the protein is folded (Röttger et al., 1998), suggesting that additional modification is required for native CatSper1 to exit the Golgi.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Röttger et al., 1998.

claim: Sialyltransferase displays maturation-associated quantitative changes in rodents.
source: In rodents, sialyltransferase displays maturation-associated quantitative changes (Ram et al., 1989; Scully and Shur, 1988) and sperm lose sialic acid from the surface during capacitation (Ma et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ram et al., 1989 and Scully and Shur, 1988.

claim: Sperm lose sialic acid from the surface during capacitation.
source: In rodents, sialyltransferase displays maturation-associated quantitative changes (Ram et al., 1989; Scully and Shur, 1988) and sperm lose sialic acid from the surface during capacitation (Ma et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ma et al., 2012.

claim: Sperm glycoproteins promote sperm migration and survival in the female reproductive tract.
source: Sperm glycoproteins promote sperm migration and survival in the female reproductive tract (Ma et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ma et al., 2016.

claim: Capacitation-associated CatSper1 degradation is blocked by incubation with a 26S proteasome inhibitor, MG-132.
source: Capacitation-associated CatSper1 degradation is blocked by incubation with a 26S proteasome inhibitor, MG-132 (Chung et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Chung et al., 2014.

claim: Calpain1 and calpain11 were detected in sperm proteome.
source: Among 15 calpain proteins identified in mammals (Ono et al., 2016), calpain1 and calpain11 were previously detected in our sperm proteome (Hwang et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ono et al., 2016 and Hwang et al., 2019.

claim: Increased Ca2+ level overrides the phosphorylation effect on calpain1 activity.
source: Increased Ca2+ level overrides the phosphorylation effect on calpain1 activity (Du et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Du et al., 2018.

claim: The protein level of CatSper2 decreases after capacitation when probed with the antibody recognizing its C-terminal domain (CTD).
source: For example, the protein level of CatSper2, but not CatSper3 or 4, also decreases after capacitation when probed with the antibody recognizing its C-terminal domain (CTD) (Figure 1; Chung et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1 and citation to Chung et al., 2014.

claim: The protein level of CatSper3 does not decrease after capacitation.
source: For example, the protein level of CatSper2, but not CatSper3 or 4, also decreases after capacitation when probed with the antibody recognizing its C-terminal domain (CTD) (Figure 1; Chung et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1 and citation to Chung et al., 2014.

claim: The protein level of CatSper4 does not decrease after capacitation.
source: For example, the protein level of CatSper2, but not CatSper3 or 4, also decreases after capacitation when probed with the antibody recognizing its C-terminal domain (CTD) (Figure 1; Chung et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1 and citation to Chung et al., 2014.

claim: pY was observed in the flagellum of mouse and human sperm interacting with the oocyte in the medium that supports sperm capacitation and fertilization in vitro.
source: Subsequently, pY was observed in the flagellum of mouse and human sperm interacting with the oocyte in the medium that supports sperm capacitation and fertilization in vitro (Sakkas et al., 2003; Urner et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Sakkas et al., 2003 and Urner et al., 2001.

claim: In sows inseminated close to ovulation, spermatozoa found in the UTJ exhibited more phosphorylation in the flagella than those bound to oviductal epithelial cells (OEC).
source: In sows inseminated close to ovulation, spermatozoa found in the UTJ exhibited more phosphorylation in the flagella than those bound to oviductal epithelial cells (OEC), where pY was limited to the equatorial region in the sperm head or no pY was observed (Luño et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Luño et al., 2013.

claim: Fer is a master kinase for capacitation-associated pY.
source: In mice, the testis-specific tyrosine kinase, Fer, is demonstrated as a master kinase for capacitation-associated pY (Alvau et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Alvau et al., 2016.

claim: Homozygous Fer-mutant male mice are fertile even though their sperm do not develop pY.
source: Surprisingly, homozygous Fer-mutant male mice are fertile even though their sperm do not develop pY.
evidence: This claim is based on the context of the discussion about Fer kinase and fertility.

claim: ROS inactivates protein tyrosine phosphatase.
source: Consistent with this idea, ROS inactivates protein tyrosine phosphatase (Tonks, 2005) and enhances pY development in sperm (Aitken et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Tonks, 2005.

claim: ROS enhances pY development in sperm.
source: Consistent with this idea, ROS inactivates protein tyrosine phosphatase (Tonks, 2005) and enhances pY development in sperm (Aitken et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Aitken et al., 1998.

claim: Inhibition of PKA anchoring to AKAPs suppresses acrosome reaction in capacitating sperm cells in vitro.
source: Inhibition of PKA anchoring to AKAPs, which induces CatSper1 truncation and degradation, also suppresses acrosome reaction in capacitating sperm cells in vitro (Stival et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Stival et al., 2018.

claim: Sperm numbers required for IVF are much higher than those observed at the fertilization site in vivo.
source: Sperm numbers required for IVF are much higher than those observed at the fertilization site in vivo (Suarez, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Suarez, 2007.

claim: Millions of spermatozoa are deposited into the cervix upon coitus in most mammals.
source: In most mammals, millions or billions of spermatozoa are deposited into the cervix upon coitus.
evidence: This is a general statement about mammalian reproduction based on established knowledge.

claim: The fertilization site is called the ampulla.
source: Yet less than 100 spermatozoa are found at the fertilization site, called the ampulla, and only 10–12 spermatozoa are observed around an oocyte (Kölle, 2015; Suarez, 2002).
evidence: This is a definitional statement about reproductive anatomy.

claim: Capacitation is a physiological process to obtain the ability to fertilize the egg.
source: Mammalian sperm undergo capacitation, a physiological process to obtain the ability to fertilize the egg, naturally inside the oviduct (Austin, 1951; Chang, 1951).
evidence: This is a definitional statement about sperm capacitation based on established knowledge and citations.

claim: The emulation of sperm capacitation in vitro led to the development of in vitro fertilization (IVF) techniques.
source: The emulation of sperm capacitation in vitro led to the development of in vitro fertilization (IVF) techniques (Steptoe and Edwards, 1976; Wang and Sauer, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Steptoe and Edwards, 1976 and Wang and Sauer, 2006.

claim: In vitro sperm capacitation does not precisely reproduce the time- and space-dependent in vivo events in the oviduct.
source: However, mounting evidence suggests that in vitro sperm capacitation does not precisely reproduce the time- and space-dependent in vivo events in the oviduct.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from multiple studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: Cholesterol shedding occurs within the plasma membrane during capacitation.
source: Cholesterol shedding and protein modifications occur within the plasma membrane (Visconti et al., 1999; Vyklicka and Lishko, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Visconti et al., 1999 and Vyklicka and Lishko, 2020.

claim: Protein modifications occur within the plasma membrane during capacitation.
source: Cholesterol shedding and protein modifications occur within the plasma membrane (Visconti et al., 1999; Vyklicka and Lishko, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Visconti et al., 1999 and Vyklicka and Lishko, 2020.

claim: Cleavage and/or degradation of intracellular proteins by individual proteases and the ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS) participate in the capacitation process.
source: Cleavage and/or degradation of intracellular proteins by individual proteases and the ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS) also participate in the capacitation process (Honda et al., 2002; Kerns et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Honda et al., 2002 and Kerns et al., 2016.

claim: Cholesterol depletion destabilizes the plasma membrane during sperm capacitation.
source: During sperm capacitation, cholesterol depletion destabilizes the plasma membrane and reorganizes the lipid raft (Nixon et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Nixon et al., 2007.

claim: Cholesterol depletion reorganizes the lipid raft during sperm capacitation.
source: During sperm capacitation, cholesterol depletion destabilizes the plasma membrane and reorganizes the lipid raft (Nixon et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Nixon et al., 2007.

claim: Caveolin-1 colocalizes with the CatSper channel complex.
source: Caveolin-1, a scaffolding protein in cholesterol-rich microdomains, colocalizes with the CatSper channel complex but does not scaffold the nanodomain (Chung et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Chung et al., 2014.

claim: Caveolin-1 does not scaffold the CatSper nanodomain.
source: Caveolin-1, a scaffolding protein in cholesterol-rich microdomains, colocalizes with the CatSper channel complex but does not scaffold the nanodomain (Chung et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Chung et al., 2014.

claim: The CatSper1 antibody used in this study is raised against the first N-terminal 150 amino acids of recombinant CatSper1.
source: The CatSper1 antibody used in this study is raised against the first N-terminal 150 amino acids of recombinant CatSper1 (Ren et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a methodological statement supported by citation to Ren et al., 2001.

claim: Loading sperm with BAPTA-AM cannot prevent the proteolytic activity under capacitating conditions.
source: This effect of Ca2+ influx by A23187 is not simply due to a rise in the intracellular Ca2+ but presumably also requires membrane events because loading sperm with BAPTA-AM cannot prevent the proteolytic activity under capacitating conditions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, bottom).
evidence: This claim is supported by experiments with BAPTA-AM shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: No more than ~15% of cells are hyperactivated in sperm capacitated in vitro.
source: Inducing sperm capacitation in vitro results in a functionally heterogeneous sperm population in which no more than ~15% of cells are hyperactivated (Neill and Olds-Clarke, 1987).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Neill and Olds-Clarke, 1987.

claim: pY mediates apoptosis in immune cells.
source: pY is reported to mediate apoptosis in immune cells (Yousefi et al., 1994) and cancer cells (Liu et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Yousefi et al., 1994.

claim: pY mediates apoptosis in cancer cells.
source: pY is reported to mediate apoptosis in immune cells (Yousefi et al., 1994) and cancer cells (Liu et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Liu et al., 1994.

claim: Capacitation-associated reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation activates intrinsic apoptotic cascade.
source: It is intriguing that capacitation-associated reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation activates intrinsic apoptotic cascade and compromises sperm motility (Koppers et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Koppers et al., 2011.

claim: Capacitation-associated reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation compromises sperm motility.
source: It is intriguing that capacitation-associated reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation activates intrinsic apoptotic cascade and compromises sperm motility (Koppers et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Koppers et al., 2011.

claim: Passive clearing of CLARITY-processed reproductive tracts from time-mated females retains the location and stability of gametes within the tract past UTJ.
source: Among tested clearing methods, we found that passive clearing of CLARITY-processed reproductive tracts from time-mated females retains the location and stability of gametes within the track past UTJ (Figure 3F–I, Figure 3—videos 4, 7 and Figure 4—video 1); whole-animal fixation by trans-cardiac perfusion perturbs minimally and rapidly arrests all cellular function while tissue-hydrogel matrix fills the lumen of the oviduct and provides supportive meshwork to prevent gamete loss during subsequent labeling steps (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3F-I, Figure 3—videos 4, 7, Figure 4—video 1, and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Whole-animal fixation by trans-cardiac perfusion perturbs minimally and rapidly arrests all cellular function.
source: Among tested clearing methods, we found that passive clearing of CLARITY-processed reproductive tracts from time-mated females retains the location and stability of gametes within the track past UTJ (Figure 3F–I, Figure 3—videos 4, 7 and Figure 4—video 1); whole-animal fixation by trans-cardiac perfusion perturbs minimally and rapidly arrests all cellular function while tissue-hydrogel matrix fills the lumen of the oviduct and provides supportive meshwork to prevent gamete loss during subsequent labeling steps (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Tissue-hydrogel matrix fills the lumen of the oviduct and provides supportive meshwork to prevent gamete loss during subsequent labeling steps.
source: Among tested clearing methods, we found that passive clearing of CLARITY-processed reproductive tracts from time-mated females retains the location and stability of gametes within the track past UTJ (Figure 3F–I, Figure 3—videos 4, 7 and Figure 4—video 1); whole-animal fixation by trans-cardiac perfusion perturbs minimally and rapidly arrests all cellular function while tissue-hydrogel matrix fills the lumen of the oviduct and provides supportive meshwork to prevent gamete loss during subsequent labeling steps (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Intact CatSper1, lack of pY, and reacted acrosome are molecular and functional signatures of most fertilizing spermatozoa in the physiological context.
source: Taken together, we conclude that intact CatSper1, lack of pY, and reacted acrosome are molecular and functional signatures of most fertilizing spermatozoa in the physiological context.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on multiple experimental results shown in Figures 2, 3, and 4.

claim: CatSper1 processing may lead to a loss of control in hyperactivation and eventually end sperm life.
source: CatSper1 processing may lead to a loss of control in hyperactivation and eventually end sperm life.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the observed correlation between CatSper1 processing and sperm function.

claim: CatSper1 is a built-in countdown timer for sperm death and elimination in the female tract.
source: Building on our observations of sperm cells from microdissection, ex vivo imaging, and CLARITY-based in situ molecular imaging (Figures 2, 3 and 4), we hypothesize that CatSper1 is a built-in countdown timer for sperm death and elimination in the female tract; CatSper1 cleavage and degradation, triggered in a time- and space-dependent manner along the female tract, signals to end sperm motility, and ultimately sets sperm lifetime in vivo.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their experimental observations.

claim: CatSper1 cleavage and degradation signals to end sperm motility.
source: Building on our observations of sperm cells from microdissection, ex vivo imaging, and CLARITY-based in situ molecular imaging (Figures 2, 3 and 4), we hypothesize that CatSper1 is a built-in countdown timer for sperm death and elimination in the female tract; CatSper1 cleavage and degradation, triggered in a time- and space-dependent manner along the female tract, signals to end sperm motility, and ultimately sets sperm lifetime in vivo.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their experimental observations.

claim: CatSper1 cleavage and degradation ultimately sets sperm lifetime in vivo.
source: Building on our observations of sperm cells from microdissection, ex vivo imaging, and CLARITY-based in situ molecular imaging (Figures 2, 3 and 4), we hypothesize that CatSper1 is a built-in countdown timer for sperm death and elimination in the female tract; CatSper1 cleavage and degradation, triggered in a time- and space-dependent manner along the female tract, signals to end sperm motility, and ultimately sets sperm lifetime in vivo.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their experimental observations.

claim: Capacitation-associated global pY development represents degenerating sperm which might concomitantly lose motility.
source: We propose that capacitation-associated global pY development represents degenerating sperm which might concomitantly lose motility.
evidence: This is a proposal by the authors based on their observations and cited literature.

claim: Escape of CatSper1 from the cleavage and subsequent degradation suppresses pY development.
source: These results suggest that escape of CatSper1 from the cleavage and subsequent degradation suppresses pY development, enabling sperm to maintain hyperactivation capability, prime AR, and achieve the fertilization in vivo.
evidence: This is a suggestion based on the observed inverse correlation between CatSper1 integrity and pY development.

claim: Escape of CatSper1 from the cleavage and subsequent degradation enables sperm to maintain hyperactivation capability.
source: These results suggest that escape of CatSper1 from the cleavage and subsequent degradation suppresses pY development, enabling sperm to maintain hyperactivation capability, prime AR, and achieve the fertilization in vivo.
evidence: This is a suggestion based on the observed correlation between CatSper1 integrity and sperm function.

claim: Escape of CatSper1 from the cleavage and subsequent degradation enables sperm to prime AR.
source: These results suggest that escape of CatSper1 from the cleavage and subsequent degradation suppresses pY development, enabling sperm to maintain hyperactivation capability, prime AR, and achieve the fertilization in vivo.
evidence: This is a suggestion based on the observed correlation between CatSper1 integrity and acrosome reaction.

claim: Escape of CatSper1 from the cleavage and subsequent degradation enables sperm to achieve fertilization in vivo.
source: These results suggest that escape of CatSper1 from the cleavage and subsequent degradation suppresses pY development, enabling sperm to maintain hyperactivation capability, prime AR, and achieve the fertilization in vivo.
evidence: This is a suggestion based on the observed characteristics of sperm in the ampulla.

claim: Mature CatSper1 in sperm contains terminal sialic acid residues.
source: We speculate that mature CatSper1 in sperm contains terminal sialic acid residues, consistent with the small drop in Catsper1 molecular weight during capacitation.
evidence: This is speculation by the authors based on the observed molecular weight changes and known biology of sialylation.

claim: The dynamic sugar modifications on CatSper1 may serve as a binding site for decapacitation factors.
source: The dynamic sugar modifications on CatSper1 may serve as a binding site for decapacitation factors and/or a recognition site during capacitation.
evidence: This is speculation by the authors about the functional role of CatSper1 glycosylation.

claim: The dynamic sugar modifications on CatSper1 may serve as a recognition site during capacitation.
source: The dynamic sugar modifications on CatSper1 may serve as a binding site for decapacitation factors and/or a recognition site during capacitation.
evidence: This is speculation by the authors about the functional role of CatSper1 glycosylation.

claim: A member of calpains might cleave CatSper1.
source: We hypothesize that a member of calpains, the Ca2+ dependent modulatory protease family, might cleave CatSper1, as their proteolytic activity can be regulated by PKA (Du et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a hypothesis by the authors based on the observed Ca2+ and PKA dependence of CatSper1 processing and citation to Du et al., 2018.

claim: Testis-specific calpain11 may target CatSper1.
source: Since recombinant CatSper1 is cleaved more specifically by sperm lysates, we propose that the testis-specific calpain11 (Ben-Aharon et al., 2006) may target CatSper1.
evidence: This is a proposal by the authors based on the specificity of CatSper1 cleavage and citation to Ben-Aharon et al., 2006.

claim: CatSper1 truncation may be coordinated with molecular changes of other CatSper subunits.
source: CatSper1 truncation may be coordinated with molecular changes of other CatSper subunits.
evidence: This is speculation by the authors about the coordinated regulation of CatSper subunits.

claim: Specific processing of the intracellular domains of pore subunits could alter the interactions with modulatory subunits and subsequent channel activity.
source: Since the cytoplasmic modulatory subunits, CatSperζ and Efcab9, mainly interact with the channel pore (Hwang et al., 2019), specific processing of the intracellular domains of pore subunits could alter the interactions and subsequent channel activity.
evidence: This is speculation by the authors based on known protein-protein interactions and citation to Hwang et al., 2019.

claim: The responsible protease is associated with the flagellar membrane but is not localized inside the CatSper nanodomains.
source: All these results corroborate our hypothesis that the responsible protease(s) is associated with the flagellar membrane but is not localized inside the CatSper nanodomains (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F); capacitation-associated membrane reorganization and the increase in local Ca2+ via the CatSper channel activates the protease(s).
evidence: This is a hypothesis by the authors based on their experimental observations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Capacitation-associated membrane reorganization and the increase in local Ca2+ via the CatSper channel activates the protease.
source: All these results corroborate our hypothesis that the responsible protease(s) is associated with the flagellar membrane but is not localized inside the CatSper nanodomains (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F); capacitation-associated membrane reorganization and the increase in local Ca2+ via the CatSper channel activates the protease(s).
evidence: This is a hypothesis by the authors based on their experimental observations.

claim: The protease pathway can be indirectly modulated by PKA via regulation of the protease activity by PKA phosphorylation of PP1/PP2A.
source: We speculate that this pathway can be indirectly modulated by PKA such as via regulation of the protease activity by PKA phosphorylation of PP1/PP2A.
evidence: This is speculation by the authors about the mechanism of PKA regulation of CatSper1 processing.

claim: CatSper-mediated Ca2+ signaling directly or indirectly contributes to sperm acrosome reaction in the female tract.
source: Thus, CatSper-mediated Ca2+ signaling directly or indirectly contributes to sperm acrosome reaction in the female tract.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observed requirement of CatSper for acrosome reaction shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Additional modification is required for native CatSper1 to exit the Golgi.
source: O-linked glycosylation takes place in the cis-Golgi for secreted and transmembrane proteins after the protein is folded (Röttger et al., 1998), suggesting that additional modification is required for native CatSper1 to exit the Golgi.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that recombinant CatSper1 cannot reach the plasma membrane and the known biology of O-glycosylation.

claim: Regulation of the proteolytic activity targeting CatSper1 involves protein phosphorylation cascades.
source: These data suggest that regulation of the proteolytic activity targeting CatSper1 involves protein phosphorylation cascades.
evidence: This is a suggestion based on the effects of PKA inhibitors and phosphatase inhibitors shown in Figure 1H.

claim: The effect of Ca2+ influx by A23187 is not simply due to a rise in the intracellular Ca2+ but presumably also requires membrane events.
source: This effect of Ca2+ influx by A23187 is not simply due to a rise in the intracellular Ca2+ but presumably also requires membrane events because loading sperm with BAPTA-AM cannot prevent the proteolytic activity under capacitating conditions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, bottom).
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of A23187 and BAPTA-AM shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: In vitro capacitation generates a heterogeneous sperm population in which intact CatSper1 and pY development are inversely correlated at the single cell level.
source: Thus far, our results suggest that in vitro capacitation generates a heterogeneous sperm population in which intact CatSper1 and pY development are inversely correlated at the single cell level.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: Heterogeneous sperm cells in vitro might reflect a collection of the time- and space-dependent changes that sperm undergo in the oviduct.
source: These heterogeneous sperm cells in vitro might reflect a collection of the time- and space-dependent changes that sperm undergo in the oviduct (Chang and Suarez, 2012; Demott and Suarez, 1992).
evidence: This is speculation by the authors based on their observations and citations to Chang and Suarez, 2012 and Demott and Suarez, 1992.

claim: The capacitation-associated changes in raft stability and distribution render CatSper1 accessible to protease activity.
source: One simple hypothesis is that the capacitation-associated changes in raft stability and distribution render CatSper1 accessible to protease activity.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors to explain CatSper1 processing during capacitation.

claim: Before inducing capacitation, CatSper1 is not processed in sperm cells, probably because the CatSper1-targeting protease activity is normally not in the immediate vicinity to the CatSper nanodomains in the flagellar membrane.
source: Before inducing capacitation, CatSper1 is not processed in sperm cells, probably because the CatSper1-targeting protease activity is normally not in the immediate vicinity to the CatSper nanodomains in the flagellar membrane (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,F).
evidence: This is speculation by the authors based on the observation that CatSper1 is not processed before capacitation.

claim: The protease activity readily cleaves CatSper1 by solubilizing the sperm membrane fraction with Triton X-100.
source: Supporting this notion, the protease activity readily cleaves CatSper1 by solubilizing the sperm membrane fraction with Triton X-100 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Calpain11 might be similarly regulated to calpain1.
source: We speculate that calpain11 might be similarly regulated to calpain1, as their domain structures and catalytic residues are conserved (Ono et al., 2016).
evidence: This is speculation by the authors based on structural similarity and citation to Ono et al., 2016.

claim: The molecular weight of recombinant CatSper1 is similar to one of the testicular forms of CatSper1.
source: It is intriguing that the molecular weight of recombinant CatSper1 is similar to one of the testicular forms of CatSper1 but bigger than that of the enzymatically deglycosylated and naked polypeptide.
evidence: This is an observation based on western blot data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The molecular weight of recombinant CatSper1 is bigger than that of the enzymatically deglycosylated and naked polypeptide.
source: It is intriguing that the molecular weight of recombinant CatSper1 is similar to one of the testicular forms of CatSper1 but bigger than that of the enzymatically deglycosylated and naked polypeptide.
evidence: This is an observation based on western blot data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The different forms of native CatSper1 may represent different degrees of glycosylation.
source: The different forms of native CatSper1 may represent different degrees of glycosylation.
evidence: This is speculation by the authors based on the observed molecular weight heterogeneity and glycosylation data.
